edits.before: Grow cordon tomatoes on a single stem for fruit from summer into autumn. Give them bright light, steady moisture and good ventilation. Pots and growbags dry out quickly.
edits.after: Greenhouse tomatoes offer flavours rarely found in shops. Cordons grow tall: train one main stem up a cane or string, removing side shoots. Bush types branch naturally; normally leave their side shoots and growing tips intact. Both need bright light, steady moisture and good ventilation. Pots and growbags dry out quickly.

edits.before: Late Feb–Mar. Late Jan only with heat and good light.
edits.after: Late Feb–Mar. Late Jan only with a heated greenhouse and bright light.

edits.before: Remove side shoots from cordons; bush types need a different routine.
edits.after: Remove side shoots from cordons; leave bush side shoots to grow.
For semi-determinate varieties, follow the seed packet.
apple or banana can help ripen the remaining tomatoes.

edits.before: A cordon tomato producing many small red cherry fruits. Complements orange Sungold with a familiar red-fruited alternative.
edits.after: A cordon with many small red cherry fruits: a red-fruited alternative to orange Sungold.

edits.before: A plum tomato for sauces and cooking. Give it warm protected conditions and distinguish it from fresh-eating cherry selections.
edits.after: A plum tomato for sauces and cooking rather than fresh salads. Give it warm, protected conditions.

edits.before: Check leaf undersides often; manage whitefly while numbers are low.
edits.after: Remove lower leaves as the plants grow tall: this aids ventilation and the extra light will help the lower fruit to ripen.

edits.before: Avoid excess high-potash feed: nutrient balance matters as much as quantity.
edits.after: Mulch soil beds and growbags with compost or well-rotted manure as the plants grow; tomatoes are heavy feeders.

edits.before: ; keep healthy leaves to feed and shade fruit.
